title: The Clinic Ledger
subtitle: A drug count that will not reconcile
briefing: A routine inspection finds that the clinic's controlled drug register does not match its stock. The shortfall has been accumulating for five months and is large enough to be criminal rather than clerical. Four members of staff hold cabinet access. All four have signed entries in the register.
solution: Sister Anne Cavanagh had been signing out doses for a patient who was discharged in March, using a paper record that was never reconciled against the electronic discharge list. Doctor Whelan's unusual prescribing pattern was a genuine clinical decision, documented in notes nobody had read, and the agency nurse's missing signature was an administrative failure rather than a theft.

suspects.name: Sister Anne Cavanagh
suspects.relation: Holds the cabinet key on days
suspects.motive: Reconciles the paper register against nothing at all.

statements.question: Who accessed the cabinet?
statements.text: All four of us, as the rota requires. Nothing unusual.

statements.question: Was a discharged patient still being dosed?
statements.text: Certainly not. We reconcile against the ward list every morning.

statements.question: Are the register entries accurate?
statements.text: They are signed and countersigned. I would stake my career on them.

suspects.name: Dr Patrick Whelan
suspects.motive: His prescribing volume is well above the regional average.

statements.question: Who accessed the cabinet?
statements.text: I sign, I do not dispense. My name is on prescriptions, not the cabinet.

statements.question: Was a discharged patient still being dosed?
statements.text: If so, nobody told me, and I would want to know.

statements.question: Are the register entries accurate?
statements.text: That is nursing's book, not mine.

suspects.name: Kelly Duarte
suspects.motive: Two of her shifts have register entries with no countersignature.

statements.question: Who accessed the cabinet?
statements.text: Me, on nights, with whoever is second on. That is the rule.

statements.question: Was a discharged patient still being dosed?
statements.text: I dose from the chart in front of me. I do not check discharges.

statements.question: Are the register entries accurate?
statements.text: Two of mine have no countersignature. I raised it and nothing happened.

suspects.name: Owen Bradach
suspects.motive: Placed three replacement orders without a matching usage record.

statements.question: Who accessed the cabinet?
statements.text: I load it on delivery days. I do not remove from it.

statements.question: Was a discharged patient still being dosed?
statements.text: I would not see that. I see quantities, not patients.

statements.question: Are the register entries accurate?
statements.text: They cannot be. I have ordered more than the register says was used.

evidence.description: The agency nurse reported missing countersignatures twice.

evidence.name: Handwriting on the charts

timeline.text: A patient is discharged from the clinic.
Dosing entries continue for that patient.
The first replacement order is placed.
An agency nurse reports missing countersignatures.
A second replacement order is placed.
A routine inspection identifies the shortfall.

hints: The register reconciles with itself. Compare it against something else.
Two suspicious patterns have documented explanations. Find the one that does not.
Ask whether every patient being dosed was still a patient.
